skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

1. # Caller Analysis: `mm::virt::manager` (`VirtMemoryManager`)
2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. 
5. Raw LSP caller-finding output: `/tmp/caller_script_out.txt` (regenerated via
6. `python scripts/find_callers_lsp.py src/kernel/src/mm/virt/manager.rs --project-dir .`).
7. 
8. Summary from the script (rust-analyzer semantic index, intra-crate `kernel`):
9. 
10. | Category | Count |
11. |----------|------:|
12. | Total exec functions | 16 |
13. | Public / trait-pub | 12 |
14. | Private | 4 |
15. | Types | 1 (`VirtMemoryManager`, 62 external refs) |
16. 
17. `VirtMemoryManager` is a **zero-sized singleton** (`struct VirtMemoryManager` with
18. unit body `Self`). All state it "manages" lives in the global
19. `PhysMemoryManager` and in the `Vmem` arguments callers pass in; the manager
20. itself is a stateless façade obtained via `VirtMemoryManager::get_mut()`.
21. 
22. ### Scope
23. 
24. In scope for top-level `#[verus_spec(...)]` (caller-before-callee), exactly:
25. 
26. | Function | Line | External callers |
27. |----------|-----:|-----------------:|
28. | `new_vmem` | 238 | 2 |
29. | `link_user_pages` | 295 | 1 |
30. | `try_resolve_cow_fault` | 526 | 1 |
31. | `try_unmap_upage` | 567 | 5 |
32. | `alloc_upages` | 595 | 5 |
33. | `ctrl_upage` | 733 | 2 |
34. | `alloc_kpage` | 755 | 3 |
35. | `alloc_kpages` | 783 | 1 |
36. | `load_elf` | 816 | 1 |
37. 
38. Out of scope (not to be modified): `init`, `get`, `get_mut`, and the private
39. helpers `new`, `link_one_user_page`, `rollback_linked_pages`,
40. `make_uninitialized_array`.
41. 
42. ### Notes on the script results
43. 
44. - **`get` has 0 external callers** — only `get_mut` (the `&mut` accessor) is used.
45.   `get` is dead/future API; out of scope regardless.
46. - One reported "external caller" each for `get_mut` / `alloc_kpage` at
47.   `mm/virt/vmem.rs:342-343` is a **false context line** (the LSP attributed a
48.   reference inside an unrelated multi-line call). The genuine call sites are
49.   listed below per function.
50. - No cross-crate callers exist: `kernel` is a leaf binary crate, so the full
51.   caller set is intra-crate and the analysis is complete.
52. 
53. ## Trait Obligations
54. 
55. None. `VirtMemoryManager` implements no traits that drive these entry points;
56. every in-scope function is an inherent `pub fn`. There are no `Drop`,
57. `GlobalAlloc`, `Iterator`, or function-pointer/closure dispatch paths into the
58. in-scope functions. (`UserFrame`/`KernelPage` `Drop` releases frames, but that is
59. internal to the value types, not a caller obligation on these functions.)
60. 
61. ## Caller Expectations
62. 
63. All callers reach the manager through
64. `let mm: &mut VirtMemoryManager = unsafe { VirtMemoryManager::get_mut() };`
65. (or receive `mm: &mut VirtMemoryManager` threaded down from there). The manager
66. carries no observable state of its own, so for every function:
67. 
68. - Callers care about the **effect on the `Vmem` argument** (and on the global
69.   physical-frame pool / refcounts) and the **`Result` discriminant**.
70. - Callers do **not** care about any field of `VirtMemoryManager` (it has none),
71.   nor about how page tables / PTE bits are laid out internally.
72. 
73. ### `new_vmem(&self, vmem: &Vmem) -> Result<Vmem, Error>`
74. 
75. Callers: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:571` (exec), `:806` (fork).
76. 
77. - Callers assume on `Ok(new)`: a fresh address space cloned from `vmem` that
78.   shares `vmem`'s **kernel** mappings and is immediately usable as a target for
79.   `load_elf` / `alloc_upages` / `link_user_pages`. `vmem` is read-only and left
80.   unchanged (`&self`, `&Vmem`).
81. - On `Err`, callers propagate with `?` and assume no new address space exists and
82.   `vmem` is untouched (no partial side effects to undo).
83. - Callers don't care: which kernel frame backs the new page directory, or how the
84.   clone copies kernel page tables.
85. 
86. ### `link_user_pages(&mut self, parent: &mut Vmem, child: &mut Vmem) -> Result<(), Error>`
87. 
88. Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:812` (fork), called immediately after
89. `new_vmem`, on a freshly created `child` that has **no overlapping user mappings**.
90. 
91. - Caller assumes on `Ok(())`: every present user page of `parent` is now mapped in
92.   `child` at the same vaddr, sharing the same physical frame with copy-on-write
93.   semantics (logically-writable pages become CoW in both `parent` and `child`;
94.   genuinely read-only pages are shared read-only). First write by either side will
95.   later be resolved by `try_resolve_cow_fault`.
96. - Caller assumes on `Err`: **full rollback** — pages already linked into `child`
97.   are unmapped (shared refcounts released) and CoW marks installed on `parent`
98.   during this call are cleared, so `parent` and `child` are restored to entry
99.   state. The caller relies on this to safely abandon the fork.
100. - Precondition the caller must uphold: `child` must not already contain user
101.   mappings overlapping `parent`'s (relied on by the rollback heuristic).
102. - Caller doesn't care: chunking strategy, AVL/CoW bit encoding, iteration order.
103. 
104. ### `try_resolve_cow_fault(&mut self, vmem: &mut Vmem, fault_addr: usize, error_code) -> Result<bool, Error>`
105. 
106. Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2897` (`handle_cow_page_fault`), forwards a CPU
107. page-fault on the running process's `vmem`. `fault_addr` need not be aligned.
108. 
109. - `Ok(true)`: fault was a CoW write; a private writable frame was installed at the
110.   faulting page and the shared frame's refcount released. Caller resumes the
111.   faulting thread.
112. - `Ok(false)`: not a CoW fault (wrong error-code bits, non-user-space address, or
113.   page not CoW). Caller forwards the fault to the registered/default handler.
114.   Importantly, **invalid/non-user addresses yield `Ok(false)`, not `Err`** — the
115.   function inspects `error_code` and rejects before mutating `vmem`.
116. - `Err`: it *was* a CoW fault but resolution failed (e.g. out of frames). Caller
117.   treats as a hard fault.
118. - Caller doesn't care: how the copy is performed or how the PTE is rewritten.
119. 
120. ### `try_unmap_upage(&mut self, vmem: &mut Vmem, vaddr) -> Result<bool, Error>`
121. 
122. Callers: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2388` (thread/stack teardown), `:2493`,
123. `:2604` (`rollback_mmap`), `:2624` (`munmap`); `pm/process/manager/unsafe.rs:406`;
124. plus internal use by `alloc_upages`'s rollback. `vaddr` is page-aligned by type.
125. 
126. - `Ok(true)`: page was present and is now unmapped; the backing user frame was
127.   released (refcount drop / free). `munmap` treats this as success.
128. - `Ok(false)`: page was **not** present — *not an error*. Teardown and rollback
129.   loops rely on this to skip never-mapped (demand-paged) pages silently; `munmap`
130.   maps it to `NoSuchEntry`.
131. - `Err`: unexpected failure; rollback callers log-and-continue, `munmap`
132.   propagates. Callers tolerate partial progress on `Err` in best-effort loops.
133. - Idempotency expectation: calling on an already-unmapped page returns
134.   `Ok(false)` (relied on by repeated rollback passes).
135. 
136. ### `alloc_upages(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access, clear, nframes, uframes: &mut Vec<UserFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
137. 
138. Callers: `mm/elf.rs:338` (segment load), `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:585,611,654`
139. (args/env/stack pages in exec), `:2566` (`do_mmap` batches).
140. 
141. - Caller-supplied-buffer contract (callers depend on it): `uframes` **must be
142.   empty** and have `capacity >= nframes`; violations return
143.   `InvalidArgument` without side effects. Callers pass `Vec::with_capacity(count)`
144.   or a reserved vec exactly for this. The vector is used only as scratch and is
145.   left empty/drained on return.
146. - On `Ok(())`: all `nframes` pages `[vaddr, vaddr + nframes*PAGE_SIZE)` are mapped
147.   with `access`; if `clear`, their contents are zeroed. The range is validated to
148.   lie entirely in user space and to be currently unmapped (`BadAddress` /
149.   `ResourceBusy` otherwise).
150. - On `Err`: **complete rollback** — any pages mapped during this call are unmapped
151.   and their frames freed, so `vmem` is unchanged from entry. Callers
152.   (`do_mmap`, exec) build their own higher-level rollback assuming each failed
153.   `alloc_upages` left nothing behind for that call.
154. - Caller doesn't care: physical frames chosen, mapping order, or how clearing is
155.   done.
156. 
157. ### `ctrl_upage(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access) -> Result<(), Error>`
158. 
159. Callers: `mm/elf.rs:304` (merge permissions for a page shared by two segments),
160. `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2642` (`mctrl`).
161. 
162. - On `Ok(())`: the already-mapped page at `vaddr` now has permissions `access`.
163. - On `Err`: permissions unchanged; caller propagates. (ELF loader relies on this
164.   to widen permissions on an overlapping page without remapping.)
165. - Caller assumes the page is already mapped (it does not allocate).
166. 
167. ### `alloc_kpage(&mut self, clear) -> Result<KernelPage, Error>`
168. 
169. Callers: `mm/kernel_vas.rs:148`, `pm/kcall/mcopy.rs:46` (scratch page).
170. 
171. - On `Ok(kpage)`: a single kernel page is returned; if `clear`, it is zeroed. The
172.   returned `KernelPage` owns its frame and **frees it on `Drop`** — `mcopy` relies
173.   on the scratch page being reclaimed when it goes out of scope.

 | Category | Count |

 unit body `Self`). All state it "manages" lives in the global
 `PhysMemoryManager` and in the `Vmem` arguments callers pass in; the manager

 ### Scope
 
 In scope for top-level `#[verus_spec(...)]` (caller-before-callee), exactly:
 
 | Function | Line | External callers |
 |----------|-----:|-----------------:|
 | `new_vmem` | 238 | 2 |
 | `link_user_pages` | 295 | 1 |
 | `try_resolve_cow_fault` | 526 | 1 |
 | `try_unmap_upage` | 567 | 5 |
 | `alloc_upages` | 595 | 5 |
 | `ctrl_upage` | 733 | 2 |
 | `alloc_kpage` | 755 | 3 |
 | `alloc_kpages` | 783 | 1 |
 | `load_elf` | 816 | 1 |
 
 Out of scope (not to be modified): `init`, `get`, `get_mut`, and the private
 helpers `new`, `link_one_user_page`, `rollback_linked_pages`,
 `make_uninitialized_array`.
 
 ### Notes on the script results
 
 - **`get` has 0 external callers** — only `get_mut` (the `&mut` accessor) is used.
   `get` is dead/future API; out of scope regardless.
 - One reported "external caller" each for `get_mut` / `alloc_kpage` at
   `mm/virt/vmem.rs:342-343` is a **false context line** (the LSP attributed a
   reference inside an unrelated multi-line call). The genuine call sites are
   listed below per function.
 - No cross-crate callers exist: `kernel` is a leaf binary crate, so the full
   caller set is intra-crate and the analysis is complete.
 
 ## Trait Obligations
 
 None. `VirtMemoryManager` implements no traits that drive these entry points;
 every in-scope function is an inherent `pub fn`. There are no `Drop`,
 `GlobalAlloc`, `Iterator`, or function-pointer/closure dispatch paths into the
 in-scope functions. (`UserFrame`/`KernelPage` `Drop` releases frames, but that is
 internal to the value types, not a caller obligation on these functions.)
 
 ## Caller Expectations
 
 All callers reach the manager through
 `let mm: &mut VirtMemoryManager = unsafe { VirtMemoryManager::get_mut() };`
 (or receive `mm: &mut VirtMemoryManager` threaded down from there). The manager
 carries no observable state of its own, so for every function:
 
 - Callers care about the **effect on the `Vmem` argument** (and on the global
   physical-frame pool / refcounts) and the **`Result` discriminant**.
 - Callers do **not** care about any field of `VirtMemoryManager` (it has none),
   nor about how page tables / PTE bits are laid out internally.
 
 ### `new_vmem(&self, vmem: &Vmem) -> Result<Vmem, Error>`
 
 Callers: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:571` (exec), `:806` (fork).
 
 - Callers assume on `Ok(new)`: a fresh address space cloned from `vmem` that
   shares `vmem`'s **kernel** mappings and is immediately usable as a target for
   `load_elf` / `alloc_upages` / `link_user_pages`. `vmem` is read-only and left
   unchanged (`&self`, `&Vmem`).
 - On `Err`, callers propagate with `?` and assume no new address space exists and
   `vmem` is untouched (no partial side effects to undo).
 - Callers don't care: which kernel frame backs the new page directory, or how the
   clone copies kernel page tables.
 
 ### `link_user_pages(&mut self, parent: &mut Vmem, child: &mut Vmem) -> Result<(), Error>`
 
 Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:812` (fork), called immediately after
 `new_vmem`, on a freshly created `child` that has **no overlapping user mappings**.
 
 - Caller assumes on `Ok(())`: every present user page of `parent` is now mapped in
   `child` at the same vaddr, sharing the same physical frame with copy-on-write
   semantics (logically-writable pages become CoW in both `parent` and `child`;
   genuinely read-only pages are shared read-only). First write by either side will
   later be resolved by `try_resolve_cow_fault`.
 - Caller assumes on `Err`: **full rollback** — pages already linked into `child`
   are unmapped (shared refcounts released) and CoW marks installed on `parent`
   during this call are cleared, so `parent` and `child` are restored to entry
   state. The caller relies on this to safely abandon the fork.
 - Precondition the caller must uphold: `child` must not already contain user
   mappings overlapping `parent`'s (relied on by the rollback heuristic).
 - Caller doesn't care: chunking strategy, AVL/CoW bit encoding, iteration order.
 
 ### `try_resolve_cow_fault(&mut self, vmem: &mut Vmem, fault_addr: usize, error_code) -> Result<bool, Error>`
 
 Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2897` (`handle_cow_page_fault`), forwards a CPU
 page-fault on the running process's `vmem`. `fault_addr` need not be aligned.
 
 - `Ok(true)`: fault was a CoW write; a private writable frame was installed at the
   faulting page and the shared frame's refcount released. Caller resumes the
   faulting thread.
 - `Ok(false)`: not a CoW fault (wrong error-code bits, non-user-space address, or
   page not CoW). Caller forwards the fault to the registered/default handler.
   Importantly, **invalid/non-user addresses yield `Ok(false)`, not `Err`** — the
   function inspects `error_code` and rejects before mutating `vmem`.
 - `Err`: it *was* a CoW fault but resolution failed (e.g. out of frames). Caller
   treats as a hard fault.
 - Caller doesn't care: how the copy is performed or how the PTE is rewritten.
 
 ### `try_unmap_upage(&mut self, vmem: &mut Vmem, vaddr) -> Result<bool, Error>`
 
 Callers: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2388` (thread/stack teardown), `:2493`,
 `:2604` (`rollback_mmap`), `:2624` (`munmap`); `pm/process/manager/unsafe.rs:406`;
 plus internal use by `alloc_upages`'s rollback. `vaddr` is page-aligned by type.
 
 - `Ok(true)`: page was present and is now unmapped; the backing user frame was
   released (refcount drop / free). `munmap` treats this as success.
 - `Ok(false)`: page was **not** present — *not an error*. Teardown and rollback
   loops rely on this to skip never-mapped (demand-paged) pages silently; `munmap`
   maps it to `NoSuchEntry`.
 - `Err`: unexpected failure; rollback callers log-and-continue, `munmap`
   propagates. Callers tolerate partial progress on `Err` in best-effort loops.
 - Idempotency expectation: calling on an already-unmapped page returns
   `Ok(false)` (relied on by repeated rollback passes).
 
 ### `alloc_upages(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access, clear, nframes, uframes: &mut Vec<UserFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
 
 Callers: `mm/elf.rs:338` (segment load), `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:585,611,654`
 (args/env/stack pages in exec), `:2566` (`do_mmap` batches).
 
 - Caller-supplied-buffer contract (callers depend on it): `uframes` **must be
   empty** and have `capacity >= nframes`; violations return
   `InvalidArgument` without side effects. Callers pass `Vec::with_capacity(count)`
   or a reserved vec exactly for this. The vector is used only as scratch and is
   left empty/drained on return.
 - On `Ok(())`: all `nframes` pages `[vaddr, vaddr + nframes*PAGE_SIZE)` are mapped
   with `access`; if `clear`, their contents are zeroed. The range is validated to
   lie entirely in user space and to be currently unmapped (`BadAddress` /
   `ResourceBusy` otherwise).
 - On `Err`: **complete rollback** — any pages mapped during this call are unmapped
   and their frames freed, so `vmem` is unchanged from entry. Callers
   (`do_mmap`, exec) build their own higher-level rollback assuming each failed
   `alloc_upages` left nothing behind for that call.
 - Caller doesn't care: physical frames chosen, mapping order, or how clearing is
   done.
 
 ### `ctrl_upage(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access) -> Result<(), Error>`
 
 Callers: `mm/elf.rs:304` (merge permissions for a page shared by two segments),
 `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:2642` (`mctrl`).
 
 - On `Ok(())`: the already-mapped page at `vaddr` now has permissions `access`.
 - On `Err`: permissions unchanged; caller propagates. (ELF loader relies on this
   to widen permissions on an overlapping page without remapping.)
 - Caller assumes the page is already mapped (it does not allocate).
 
 ### `alloc_kpage(&mut self, clear) -> Result<KernelPage, Error>`
 
 Callers: `mm/kernel_vas.rs:148`, `pm/kcall/mcopy.rs:46` (scratch page).
 
 - On `Ok(kpage)`: a single kernel page is returned; if `clear`, it is zeroed. The
   returned `KernelPage` owns its frame and **frees it on `Drop`** — `mcopy` relies
   on the scratch page being reclaimed when it goes out of scope.
 - On `Err`: no page allocated; caller propagates with `?`.
 
 ### `alloc_kpages(&mut self, clear, count, kframes: &mut Vec<KernelFrame>) -> Result<(), Error>`
 
 Caller: `mm/kstack.rs:95` (kernel stack frames).
 
 - Same caller-supplied-buffer contract as `alloc_upages`: `kframes` must be empty
   with `capacity >= count` (else `InvalidArgument`).
 - On `Ok(())`: `kframes` holds exactly `count` contiguous kernel frames; if
   `clear`, each is zeroed. The caller then maps them
   (`map(KernelPage::new)`) into a kernel stack.
 - On `Err`: `kframes` is left empty (allocated frames dropped/freed); no leak.
 
 ### `load_elf(&mut self, vmem, elf: &Elf32Fhdr) -> Result<(VirtualAddress, PageAligned<VirtualAddress>), Error>`
 
 Caller: `pm/process/manager/mod.rs:575` (exec), on a freshly created `vmem`.
 
 - On `Ok((entry, args_vaddr))`: ELF segments are loaded/mapped into `vmem`;
   `entry` is the program entry point used to forge the user context, and
   `args_vaddr` is a page-aligned address where the caller then allocates a page
   for argv (via `alloc_upages`). Caller assumes both are valid user-space
   addresses for the loaded image.
 - On `Err`: caller abandons the new `vmem` (`?`); partial mappings inside `vmem`
   are acceptable because the whole address space is discarded on failure.
 - Caller doesn't care: segment layout, how `elf32_load` maps each PT_LOAD, or
   where `args_vaddr` is placed relative to segments.
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 From the caller's perspective, `VirtMemoryManager` is a **stateless service
 (singleton façade) for managing user/kernel page mappings inside a `Vmem` address
 space**, drawing physical frames from the global physical-memory pool. Callers use
 it to: create/clone address spaces (`new_vmem`), populate them
 (`load_elf`, `alloc_upages`, `link_user_pages`), change/remove user mappings
 (`ctrl_upage`, `try_unmap_upage`), resolve copy-on-write faults
 (`try_resolve_cow_fault`), and obtain kernel-side pages/frames
 (`alloc_kpage`, `alloc_kpages`).
 
 ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
 
 - **Transactional on failure.** Mapping operations either fully succeed or fully
   roll back: `alloc_upages`, `alloc_kpages`, and `link_user_pages` leave their
   target `Vmem` (and frame refcounts) as if never called when they return `Err`.
 - **`Ok(false)` ≠ error.** For `try_unmap_upage` and `try_resolve_cow_fault`,
   `Ok(false)` denotes a benign "nothing to do / not applicable" outcome that
   callers branch on; only `Err` is a real failure.
 - **Caller-owned scratch buffers** (`uframes`, `kframes`) must be empty with
   sufficient capacity; the manager validates this and never reallocates them.
 - **Frame ownership flows through RAII.** Returned `KernelPage`/`UserFrame` (and
   those dropped during unmap/rollback) release physical frames on `Drop`; callers
   rely on scope-based reclamation, never manual frees.
 - **User-space confinement.** User-page operations validate that addresses lie in
   the user region; out-of-range inputs yield `BadAddress`/`Ok(false)` rather than
   corrupting kernel mappings.

   itself; every effect is on the passed-in `Vmem` or the global frame pool, so the

1. # View Design: `mm::virt::manager` (`VirtMemoryManager`)
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. To callers, `VirtMemoryManager` is a **stateless singleton service** that
6. mediates page-mapping operations on virtual address spaces (`Vmem`) and hands
7. out kernel-side pages/frames drawn from the global physical-frame pool. It is
8. obtained via `VirtMemoryManager::get_mut()` and threaded as `&mut self`, but
9. `struct VirtMemoryManager;` is **zero-sized**: it owns no fields and carries no
10. observable state of its own (caller analysis §"Manager statelessness").
11. 
12. Consequently the abstraction boundary for this module is **not** a field-bearing
13. manager View. Every observable effect lands on one of:
14. 
15. 1. the **`Vmem` argument(s)** a function receives — modeled by the *inherited*
16.    `VmemView` already designed and implemented for the `mm::virt::vmem` module;
17. 2. the **returned owned RAII values** (`KernelPage`, `Vec<KernelFrame>`,
18.    `Vec<UserFrame>`, the new `Vmem` from `new_vmem`) — modeled by their own
19.    type-level views; and
20. 3. the **global physical-frame pool** behind `PhysMemoryManager` — a *global*
21.    resource, deliberately left **outside** any single View (parallel to the way
22.    `VmemView` excludes the global CR3 register and global physical memory; see
23.    Rejected Alternatives).
24. 
25. So this phase delivers three things: (a) a **unit** manager View, (b) a
26. re-evaluation of the **inherited `VmemView`** against the manager's callers, and
27. (c) the **manager-level spec vocabulary** (pure architectural predicates +
28. composite transitions over `VmemView`) that the manager's contracts will speak.
29. 
30. ---
31. 
32. ## View Struct
33. 
34. The manager holds no state, so its View is a marker (unit) type. The
35. substitution test forces this: a field-bearing manager View could only mirror
36. the global `PhysMemoryManager` or a registry of live `Vmem`s — neither of which
37. the manager *owns* or a caller *observes through `&mut self`*.
38. 
39. ```rust
40. verus! {
41. 
42. /// Abstract state of the (stateless) virtual-memory manager singleton.
43. ///
44. /// `VirtMemoryManager` is zero-sized: it owns no mappings, no frames, and no
45. /// page tables. All abstract state a caller reasons about lives in the `Vmem`
46. /// argument(s) (`VmemView`) and in the returned owned values. This marker view
47. /// therefore carries no fields — it exists only so callers can write `self@`
48. /// and so the manager satisfies the module's View/`inv()` contract.
49. pub struct VirtMemoryManagerView;
50. 
51. } // verus!
52. ```
53. 
54. Spec functions to be implemented in `manager.spec.rs` (signatures + intent
55. designed here; bodies reference impl state and are filled in the specification
56. phase):
57. 
58. - `view(&self) -> VirtMemoryManagerView` — `pub closed spec fn`. Maps the
59.   zero-sized exec singleton to the unit View. Closed by convention; there is no
60.   internal field mapping to leak.
61. - `internal_inv(&self) -> bool` — `pub closed spec fn`, placeholder `true`. The
62.   manager has no internal exec fields, so there is no implementation-consistency
63.   obligation to encode. (The "manager is initialized" property guarded by
64.   `MEMORY_MANAGER_INIT` is established by `init`/`get_mut`, both out of scope,
65.   and is not a precondition of the in-scope methods — they already hold a valid
66.   `&mut self`.)
67. - `inv(&self) -> bool` — `pub open spec fn`, `self.internal_inv()` (i.e. `true`).
68.   There is no caller-visible manager-level well-formedness; the well-formedness
69.   that matters is per-`Vmem` (`vmem.inv() == vmem@.inv()`) and is asserted on the
70.   `Vmem` arguments in each method's `requires`/`ensures`, **not** on `self`.
71. 
72. Because `self@` is unit, every method trivially satisfies `self@ == old(self)@`;
73. that clause is therefore omitted from the manager's contracts (it carries no
74. information). The manager View appears in specs only to satisfy the module
75. convention.
76. 
77. ---
78. 
79. ## Inherited View: `VmemView` (re-evaluated against manager callers)
80. 
81. The central abstraction the manager's specs reference is the upstream
82. `VmemView` (from `mm::virt::vmem`, already implemented in `vmem.spec.rs`):
83. 
84. ```rust
85. pub struct PagePerms   { pub read: bool, pub write: bool, pub exec: bool }
86. pub struct UserPageView { pub frame: nat, pub perms: PagePerms, pub cow: bool }
87. pub struct KernelPageView { pub frame: nat, pub perms: PagePerms }
88. pub struct VmemView {
89.     pub user:   Map<nat, UserPageView>,   // present user pages: vaddr -> mapping
90.     pub kernel: Map<nat, KernelPageView>, // present kernel pages: vaddr -> mapping
91.     pub pgdir:  nat,                       // page-directory physical base (CR3)
92. }
93. ```
94. 
95. with the free architectural predicates (`spec_is_user_addr`,
96. `spec_is_user_region`, `spec_is_physical_region`, `is_page_aligned`,
97. `page_base`, `page_offset`, `PAGE_SIZE`, `USER_BASE`, `USER_END`) and the
98. permission map `AccessPermission::perms_view() -> PagePerms`.
99. 
100. **Substitution-test re-evaluation of each inherited field, from each manager
101. caller's perspective** (the skill requires checking the inherited View against
102. *all* callers, not just the original one):
103. 
104. | Inherited field | Manager callers that observe it | Survives substitution? |
105. |---|---|---|
106. | `user: Map<nat, UserPageView>` | `alloc_upages` (insert a contiguous run), `try_unmap_upage` (remove), `ctrl_upage` (perms), `link_user_pages` (copy parent→child as CoW), `try_resolve_cow_fault` (privatize one page), `load_elf` (grow), `new_vmem` (child starts empty) | ✅ every address space maps user vaddrs→frames regardless of page-table representation |
107. | `UserPageView.frame` | CoW sharing in `link_user_pages` (child frame == parent frame), privatization in `try_resolve_cow_fault` (new frame ≠ old), released frame on `try_unmap_upage` | ✅ a mapping is backed by *some* physical frame; the walk mechanism is irrelevant |
108. | `UserPageView.perms` | `alloc_upages`/`ctrl_upage` set `access.perms_view()`; the CoW invariant hinges on `write` | ✅ permissions are architectural, not layout-specific |
109. | `UserPageView.cow` | toggled by `link_user_pages` (mark) and `try_resolve_cow_fault` (clear); decides whether a write faults | ✅ CoW is a semantic state every implementation must track |
110. | `kernel: Map<…>` | `new_vmem` shares the parent's kernel half into the child; otherwise read-only here | ✅ kernel↦frame mapping exists in any design |
111. | `pgdir: nat` | `new_vmem` guarantees the child's base ≠ parent's | ✅ every address space has a root with a physical base |
112. 
113. **Verdict:** the inherited `VmemView` is **complete and sound for all manager
114. callers** — no field is renamed, removed, or added. It already exposes exactly
115. the user/kernel mapping structure, frames, permissions, CoW marks, and
116. page-directory base that the nine manager entry points need. What the manager
117. phase *adds* is not new View state but new **vocabulary** (below) that composes
118. the existing `VmemView` transitions into the larger, range- and fork-shaped
119. operations the manager performs.
120. 
121. ---
122. 
123. ## Manager-level Spec Vocabulary
124. 
125. These are the abstraction the manager contributes. They are **free
126. `pub open spec fn`s in `manager.spec.rs`** over the inherited `VmemView` and
127. architectural types — *not* extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl VirtMemoryManager`
128. (the exec type keeps only `inv`/`view`), and not edits to `VmemView` (owned by
129. the vmem module). They are the building blocks for the `requires`/`ensures` of
130. the in-scope functions.
131. 
132. ### Pure architectural predicates (no `&self`, instance-independent)
133. 
134. ```rust
135. verus! {
136. 
137. /// A page fault qualifies as a copy-on-write write fault: a user-mode write to
138. /// a present page. Pure decode of the x86 page-fault error-code bits
139. /// (`is_present`/`is_write`/`is_user` are pure `const fn`s in arch::cpu::excp).
140. /// Whether the *page* is actually CoW is then read from `vmem@` separately.
141. pub open spec fn spec_is_cow_write_fault(ec: ErrorCode) -> bool {
142.     ec.is_present() && ec.is_write() && ec.is_user()
143. }

333. 
334. **Why a unit manager View (substitution test on the *whole* View).** Rewriting
335. `VirtMemoryManager` with a completely different allocation algorithm changes
336. nothing observable through `&mut self`, because the type is zero-sized and every
337. effect is routed to a `Vmem` argument, a returned value, or the global pool. A
338. field-bearing manager View would therefore mirror state the manager does not
339. own — failing the substitution test by construction. The caller analysis reaches
340. the same conclusion: "the View must model the address space / frame ownership,
341. not the (empty) manager."
342. 
343. **Why reuse `VmemView` unchanged.** The manager is a thin orchestration layer
344. over `Vmem`'s primitives (`map`, `unmap`, `uctrl`, `mark_cow`, `resolve_cow`,
345. `clone`, …). Its callers observe address-space *effects*, which `VmemView`
346. already abstracts exactly (mapping structure + frames + perms + CoW + pgdir).
347. Re-checking each field against all nine entry points (table above) found no gap
348. and no leak, so the honest action is **keep all, rename none, add none**.
349. 
350. **Why the new vocabulary lives as free spec fns over `VmemView`.** The manager
351. performs *range* (`alloc_upages`) and *fork* (`link_user_pages`) operations that
352. have no single-page inherited transition. Encoding their success/precondition
353. shapes as named predicates (`maps_user_run_with`, `region_user_unmapped`,
354. `links_child_cow`, `link_user_pages_pre`, `logically_writable`) keeps each
355. contract declarative and lets the spec phase reuse the same names in `Ok`
356. clauses and rollback (`Err ⟹ old@ == new@`) reasoning. They take `VmemView` by
357. value (not `&self` on the manager), and are defined in `manager.spec.rs` so the
358. vmem module is not modified — respecting the skill's "no extra pub spec fns on
359. `impl MyType`" rule for the exec manager type.
360. 
361. **Why `spec_is_cow_write_fault` is a free predicate.** Classifying an
362. `ErrorCode` (present ∧ write ∧ user) is a pure function of the architectural
363. error-code bits — instance-independent, no `&self` — exactly like the inherited
364. `spec_is_user_addr` family. It belongs as a free spec fn, not as View state.
365. 
366. **Frames/RAII are observed through domain membership, not refcounts.** As in the
367. vmem design, ownership balance (no leak / no double-free) is enforced by Rust's
368. type system (`UserFrame`/`KernelFrame`/`KernelPage` by-value transfer + `Drop`)
369. and reflected abstractly by `user`-domain changes and by `kframes@.len()` /
370. returned-value validity. No refcount field is introduced.
371. 
372. ---
373. 
374. ## Rejected Alternatives
375. 
376. 1. **A field-bearing manager View mirroring `PhysMemoryManager`** (e.g.
377.    `free_frames: Set<nat>`, `refcounts: Map<nat,nat>`). *Rejected.* The pool is
378.    *global* mutable state reached via `PhysMemoryManager::get_mut()`, not owned
379.    by the manager nor reachable through its `&mut self`. Threading a ghost pool
380.    through a zero-sized `&mut self` models fiction and couples the View to the
381.    allocator's `Rc`/free-list strategy — failing the substitution test. It also
382.    provides no fact any *caller* observes: `alloc_kpage` callers see only the
383.    returned page and `Ok`/`Err`. Pool depletion is a liveness property handled
384.    (if ever) by a separate global frame-pool abstraction. This mirrors
385.    `VmemView` rejecting a global CR3 field and global physical-memory contents.
386. 
387. 2. **Modeling kernel-frame allocation as a manager-View transition.**
388.    *Rejected.* `alloc_kpage`/`alloc_kpages` touch no `Vmem` and produce owned
389.    RAII values whose validity (page-aligned, within `PHYS_MEM_SIZE`, cleared)
390.    is a property of `KernelPage`/`KernelFrame`'s **own** type views. Pinning
391.    *which* frame is chosen would over-specify an allocator detail callers
392.    explicitly do not care about (caller analysis §`alloc_kpage`).
393. 
394. 3. **A registry of live `Vmem`s inside the manager View** (e.g.
395.    `spaces: Map<id, VmemView>`). *Rejected.* The manager never holds a
396.    collection of address spaces; callers pass exactly the `Vmem`(s) they own
397.    into each call. The relevant state is the argument's `VmemView`, asserted in
398.    `requires`/`ensures`, not a manager-held set. A registry would duplicate
399.    caller-owned state and break View consistency.

 > bit off — so the write→read-only rewrite is implied, not restated. The
 > specification phase may pin the exact parent rewrite using the inherited
 > `spec_mark_cow` transition; the caller-visible facts (child shares the same
 > frame at the same vaddr; logically-writable pages are CoW in both) are fully
 > captured above.
 
 For the single-page operations the manager already has exact inherited
 transitions and needs **no new** composite:
 
 | Manager op | Inherited `VmemView` transition reused |
 |---|---|
 | `try_unmap_upage` (true) | `old@.spec_unmap(v)` |
 | `ctrl_upage` | `old@.spec_uctrl(v, access.perms_view())` |
 | `try_resolve_cow_fault` (true) | `exists f. old@.spec_resolve_cow(v, f)` |
 | `new_vmem` child kernel/user/pgdir | direct field reads (`kernel`, `user.is_empty()`, `pgdir`) |
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec sketches per top-level entry point
 
 (Contracts are written in the specification phase; these sketches prove every
 piece of vocabulary above is exercised and that `VmemView` suffices.)
 
 - **`new_vmem(&self, vmem: &Vmem) -> Result<Vmem, Error>`** — `requires
   vmem.inv()`. `Ok(new)` ⟹ `new.inv()` ∧ `new@.kernel == vmem@.kernel` ∧
   `new@.user == Map::empty()` ∧ `new@.pgdir != vmem@.pgdir`. `vmem` is `&`, so
   `vmem@` unchanged. `Err` ⟹ no new space; `vmem@` unchanged.
 
 - **`link_user_pages(&mut self, parent, child) -> Result<(), Error>`** —
   `requires parent.inv() && child.inv() && link_user_pages_pre(parent@, child@)`.
   `Ok(())` ⟹ `links_child_cow(old(parent)@, parent@, old(child)@, child@)` ∧
   `parent.inv() && child.inv()`. `Err` ⟹ **full rollback**:
   `parent@ == old(parent)@ && child@ == old(child)@`.
 
 - **`try_resolve_cow_fault(&mut self, vmem, fault_addr, error_code)
   -> Result<bool, Error>`** — `requires vmem.inv()`; let
   `v = page_base(fault_addr)`. `Ok(true)` ⟹ `spec_is_cow_write_fault(error_code)`
   ∧ `old(vmem)@.user.contains_key(v)` ∧ `old(vmem)@.user[v].cow` ∧
   `exists f. spec_is_physical_region(f, PAGE_SIZE) && vmem@ == old(vmem)@.spec_resolve_cow(v, f)`.
   `Ok(false)` ⟹ `(!spec_is_cow_write_fault(error_code) || !spec_is_user_addr(v)
   || !old(vmem)@.user.contains_key(v) || !old(vmem)@.user[v].cow)` ∧
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@`. `Err` ⟹ it *was* a CoW fault but resolution failed;
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@`. (Note: invalid/non-user addresses yield `Ok(false)`,
   never `Err` — caller analysis §`try_resolve_cow_fault`.)
 
 - **`try_unmap_upage(&mut self, vmem, vaddr) -> Result<bool, Error>`** —
   `requires vmem.inv()`. `Ok(true)` ⟹ `old(vmem)@.user.contains_key(vaddr@)` ∧
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@.spec_unmap(vaddr@)`. `Ok(false)` ⟹
   `!old(vmem)@.user.contains_key(vaddr@)` ∧ `vmem@ == old(vmem)@` (benign,
   idempotent). `Err` ⟹ best-effort; abstract state may be partially changed but
   `vmem.inv()` holds.
 
 - **`alloc_upages(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access, clear, nframes, uframes)
   -> Result<(), Error>`** — `requires vmem.inv() && uframes@.len() == 0 &&
   uframes.capacity() >= nframes`. (Buffer-contract violation ⟹ `InvalidArgument`,
   no side effects.) `Ok(())` ⟹
   `maps_user_run_with(old(vmem)@, vmem@, vaddr@, nframes as nat, access.perms_view())`
   ∧ `vmem.inv()` ∧ `uframes@.len() == 0`. `Err` ⟹ **complete rollback**:
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@` ∧ `uframes@.len() == 0`. (Precondition
   `region_user_unmapped(old(vmem)@, vaddr@, nframes)` is the static
   characterization; the runtime `BadAddress`/`ResourceBusy` checks discharge the
   dynamic part — see `spec-design` "static vs dynamic".)
 
 - **`ctrl_upage(&mut self, vmem, vaddr, access) -> Result<(), Error>`** —
   `requires vmem.inv() && vmem@.user.contains_key(vaddr@)` (page already mapped;
   it does not allocate). `Ok(())` ⟹
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@.spec_uctrl(vaddr@, access.perms_view())`. `Err` ⟹
   `vmem@ == old(vmem)@`.
 
 - **`alloc_kpage(&mut self, clear) -> Result<KernelPage, Error>`** — no `Vmem`.
   `Ok(kpage)` ⟹ `kpage` owns a valid, page-aligned physical frame
   (`spec_is_physical_region(kpage@.frame, PAGE_SIZE)`; cleared if `clear`),
   released on `Drop`. `Err` ⟹ nothing allocated. Manager View unaffected.
   (Frame validity is a property of `KernelPage`'s own type view; the global pool
   is external — see Rejected Alternatives.)
 
 - **`alloc_kpages(&mut self, clear, count, kframes) -> Result<(), Error>`** —
   `requires kframes@.len() == 0 && kframes.capacity() >= count`. `Ok(())` ⟹
   `kframes@.len() == count` ∧ each entry a valid page-aligned physical frame
   (cleared if `clear`). `Err` ⟹ `kframes@.len() == 0` (allocated frames
   dropped/freed; no leak).
 
 - **`load_elf(&mut self, vmem, elf) -> Result<(VirtualAddress,
   PageAligned<VirtualAddress>), Error>`** — `requires vmem.inv()`.
   `Ok((entry, args_vaddr))` ⟹ `vmem.inv()` ∧ user domain grew
   (`old(vmem)@.user.dom().subset_of(vmem@.user.dom())`) ∧ kernel half & pgdir
   unchanged ∧ `spec_is_user_addr(entry@)` ∧ `spec_is_user_addr(args_vaddr@)` ∧
   `is_page_aligned(args_vaddr@)`. `Err` ⟹ **no rollback guarantee** — partial
   mappings inside `vmem` are acceptable because the caller discards the whole
   `vmem` (`?`); we still guarantee `vmem.inv()`. (Per-segment layout is an ELF
   detail the caller does not depend on — caller analysis §`load_elf`.)
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale
 
 **Why a unit manager View (substitution test on the *whole* View).** Rewriting
 `VirtMemoryManager` with a completely different allocation algorithm changes
 nothing observable through `&mut self`, because the type is zero-sized and every
 effect is routed to a `Vmem` argument, a returned value, or the global pool. A
 field-bearing manager View would therefore mirror state the manager does not
 own — failing the substitution test by construction. The caller analysis reaches
 the same conclusion: "the View must model the address space / frame ownership,
 not the (empty) manager."
 
 **Why reuse `VmemView` unchanged.** The manager is a thin orchestration layer
 over `Vmem`'s primitives (`map`, `unmap`, `uctrl`, `mark_cow`, `resolve_cow`,
 `clone`, …). Its callers observe address-space *effects*, which `VmemView`
 already abstracts exactly (mapping structure + frames + perms + CoW + pgdir).
 Re-checking each field against all nine entry points (table above) found no gap
 and no leak, so the honest action is **keep all, rename none, add none**.
 
 **Why the new vocabulary lives as free spec fns over `VmemView`.** The manager
 performs *range* (`alloc_upages`) and *fork* (`link_user_pages`) operations that
 have no single-page inherited transition. Encoding their success/precondition
 shapes as named predicates (`maps_user_run_with`, `region_user_unmapped`,
 `links_child_cow`, `link_user_pages_pre`, `logically_writable`) keeps each
 contract declarative and lets the spec phase reuse the same names in `Ok`
 clauses and rollback (`Err ⟹ old@ == new@`) reasoning. They take `VmemView` by
 value (not `&self` on the manager), and are defined in `manager.spec.rs` so the
 vmem module is not modified — respecting the skill's "no extra pub spec fns on
 `impl MyType`" rule for the exec manager type.
 
 **Why `spec_is_cow_write_fault` is a free predicate.** Classifying an
 `ErrorCode` (present ∧ write ∧ user) is a pure function of the architectural
 error-code bits — instance-independent, no `&self` — exactly like the inherited
 `spec_is_user_addr` family. It belongs as a free spec fn, not as View state.
 
 **Frames/RAII are observed through domain membership, not refcounts.** As in the
 vmem design, ownership balance (no leak / no double-free) is enforced by Rust's
 type system (`UserFrame`/`KernelFrame`/`KernelPage` by-value transfer + `Drop`)
 and reflected abstractly by `user`-domain changes and by `kframes@.len()` /
 returned-value validity. No refcount field is introduced.
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 1. **A field-bearing manager View mirroring `PhysMemoryManager`** (e.g.
    `free_frames: Set<nat>`, `refcounts: Map<nat,nat>`). *Rejected.* The pool is
    *global* mutable state reached via `PhysMemoryManager::get_mut()`, not owned
    by the manager nor reachable through its `&mut self`. Threading a ghost pool
    through a zero-sized `&mut self` models fiction and couples the View to the
    allocator's `Rc`/free-list strategy — failing the substitution test. It also
    provides no fact any *caller* observes: `alloc_kpage` callers see only the
    returned page and `Ok`/`Err`. Pool depletion is a liveness property handled
    (if ever) by a separate global frame-pool abstraction. This mirrors
    `VmemView` rejecting a global CR3 field and global physical-memory contents.
 
 2. **Modeling kernel-frame allocation as a manager-View transition.**
    *Rejected.* `alloc_kpage`/`alloc_kpages` touch no `Vmem` and produce owned
    RAII values whose validity (page-aligned, within `PHYS_MEM_SIZE`, cleared)
    is a property of `KernelPage`/`KernelFrame`'s **own** type views. Pinning
    *which* frame is chosen would over-specify an allocator detail callers
    explicitly do not care about (caller analysis §`alloc_kpage`).
 
 3. **A registry of live `Vmem`s inside the manager View** (e.g.
    `spaces: Map<id, VmemView>`). *Rejected.* The manager never holds a
    collection of address spaces; callers pass exactly the `Vmem`(s) they own
    into each call. The relevant state is the argument's `VmemView`, asserted in
    `requires`/`ensures`, not a manager-held set. A registry would duplicate
    caller-owned state and break View consistency.

---
name: spec-design
description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
   5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
      assumption was checked against.

   - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
     Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
     verification.
   
   `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
   must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.
4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
   spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
   (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
   what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
   (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
   (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:

   Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
   ```
   self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,
   // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
   ```
   Good (complete by construction):
   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```
   This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
   inline or via spec transition functions.
7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
   prevents accidentally omitting one arm:

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures
       result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
   ```
   Good:
   ```
   ensures match result {

 # Spec Design Guide
 
 ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
 
 ### Qualities of a Good Spec
 
 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
    verifies the copy, not the real code.
 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
    recursive spec functions.
 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
 
 ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
 
 If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
 nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
 spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
 design model.
 
 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
    annotation beats no annotation.
 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
    Always search vstd first.
 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
    by vstd.
    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
    make Verus pass.
    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
 
 ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
 
 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
    
    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
    spec or proof instead.
    
    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
 
    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
 
    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
       in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
       `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
       reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
       Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
       requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
    2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
       guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
       guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
       Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
       clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
       callers will not check it.
    3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
       compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
       explicitly in the spec.
    4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
       the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
       code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"
    5. **Version sensitivity**: note the stdlib/crate version the
       assumption was checked against.
 
    - `external_body`: allowed on dependency functions in other modules as
      a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
      and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.
      Never use `external_body` on the current module's own functions to skip
      verification.
    
    `assume_specification` and `axiom` are unverified axioms.
    See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.
 3. **Missing Loop Specs** — loops need `invariant` clauses that capture
    the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
    loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
    it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
    or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant
    must be strong enough that, combined with the loop exit condition, it
    implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
    strengthened later — that is expected.
 4. **Code-as-Spec / Operational Spec** — restating implementation logic
    or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in
    spec. Good: `is_sorted(result@) && is_permutation_of(result@, input@)`.
 5. **One-Sided Error Spec** — only specifies success, says nothing
    (or `true`) about failure. Error paths need equal rigor.
 6. **Missing Frame Condition / Field-by-Field Conjunction** — ensures says
    what changed but not what didn't, OR lists unchanged fields one by one
    (fragile — easy to forget a field). **Always use struct update syntax**
    (`..old(self)@`) so completeness is guaranteed by construction:
 
    Bad (fragile — silent field omission):
    ```
    self@.field_a == old(self)@.field_a,
    self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
    self@.field_c == new_value,
    // forgot field_d — spec is incomplete!
    ```
    Good (complete by construction):
    ```
    self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
    ```
    This applies everywhere state changes appear in ensures — whether
    inline or via spec transition functions.
 7. **Separate Ok/Err Conditions** — using `result.is_ok() ==> ...` and
    `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
    single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and
    prevents accidentally omitting one arm:
 
    Bad:
    ```
    ensures
        result.is_ok() ==> /* success postcondition */,
        result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
    ```
    Good:
    ```
    ensures match result {
        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
        Err(e) => self@ == old(self)@,
    }
    ```
 8. **Tautological Postconditions** — trivially true for any return value.
 9. **Subsumed Properties** — logically implied by a stronger property
    already present. Before adding an ensures clause, check: is this
    derivable from `self.inv()` combined with the other ensures? If so,
    delete it — redundant clauses obscure the spec's intent and make
    reviews harder.
 10. **Over-specification** — forcing a particular implementation strategy.
    Only add specificity when callers genuinely depend on it.
 11. **Scattered Invariant** — the same property appears in `requires` of
     every (or nearly every) method. A universally required property is an
     invariant — move it to `inv()` and maintain it in `ensures`.
 12. **`uninterp` as Verification Escape** — using `uninterp spec fn` to
     avoid writing a concrete spec definition, then injecting properties
     via `external_body` proof axioms. This combination is equivalent to
     `assume` — it introduces unverified assumptions about a function
     whose behavior is entirely under our control.
     `uninterp spec fn` is banned. All spec functions must have concrete
     definitions. If `uninterp` appears on `View::view()` of an
     `external_body` type, that is a mechanical consequence of the type
     being `external_body` — the trust obligation is tracked there, not
     as a separate `uninterp` allowance. If a spec function is hard to
     define concretely, that is a signal to simplify the abstraction,
     not to use `uninterp`.
 
 ### Error Path Spec Principles
 
 Every function that can fail should specify **what happens on failure**
 with the same rigor as the success path.
 
 1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
 2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract
    predicates on the module's interface state, not as a list of individual
    code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
    impossible?
 3. **Liveness** — if the preconditions and current state make success
    possible, the spec must guarantee success (i.e., the function must
    not spuriously return `None`/`Err`). A spec that *allows* failure
    even when success is achievable is under-specified — callers cannot
    rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:
    ```
    ensures match result {
        Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
        Err(e) => /* error postcondition */,
    }
    ```
    This makes both arms visible for review — neither path is silently omitted.
 
 ### Where NOT to Invest Spec Effort
 
 **Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
 - **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
 - **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
 - **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations
 
 **Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
 - **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
   `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
   warrant no further properties.
 - **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
   verified function with no additional logic.
 
 ### Property Coverage Checklist
 
 When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
 function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.
 
 1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
    - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
    - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
    - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms

262. 2. **Safety** — What must never happen?
263.    - Bounds, disjointness, uniqueness, conservation, injectivity, ordering, monotonicity
264. 
265. 3. **Liveness** — What good things must happen?
266.    - Guaranteed success conditions, resource availability, recoverability

268. 4. **Structural Consistency** — Is the data self-consistent?

271. ### Invariant Design
272. 
273. Two kinds of invariants appear during specification:
274. 
275. - **Type invariant (`inv()`)** — defined on the View type (see **view-design**
276.   skill). Every constructor must establish it; every method must preserve it.
277.   If a property appears in `requires` of nearly every method, it belongs in
278.   `inv()` instead.
279. - **Loop invariant** — defined on loops. Must hold on entry (base case),
280.   be preserved by each iteration (inductive step), and together with the
281.   exit condition imply the function's `ensures` (sufficiency). Define
282.   complex invariants as `spec fn` predicates rather than inline clauses.
283. 
284. Both should reference View fields and abstract state, not implementation
285. details.
286. 
287. ### Static vs Dynamic Condition Enforcement
288. 
289. **Key question**: Can this runtime check be statically eliminated through
290. verification?
291. 
292. **Yes → add `requires`**. The condition is provable from caller context
293. (e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
294. insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
295. once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.
296. 
297. **No → keep runtime check + Err**. The condition depends on inherently
298. dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
299. operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
300. `requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.
301. 
302. **Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
303. runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
304. `// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
305. verification work knows to clean it up.

307. ### Post-Generation Spec Refinement
308. 
309. After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
310. The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
311. find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**
312. 
313. 1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
314.    that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
315.    it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
316. 2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
317.    clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
318. 3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
319.    proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
320.    form the caller actually needs.

324. ## Part 2: Spec Classification
325. 
326. Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:
327. 
328. ### Internal
329. 
330. Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
331. invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
332. **The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
333. correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
334. provides direct feedback.
335. 
336. ### External-top (API contracts)
337. 
338. Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
339. callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.
340. 
341. ### External-bottom (trust assumptions)
342. 
343. Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
344. behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
345. These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
346. may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
347. `external_body`, and `axiom`. Which functions belong in this category
348. is pre-determined by the TCB allowed list — do not make new trust
349. boundary decisions during specification or proving.
350. 
351. ### Rules
352. 
353. - The caller analysis and View design identify external-top properties.
354. - Trust boundary decisions (which functions get `external_body`) are
355.   pre-approved in the TCB allowed list. Do not classify new functions
356.   as trust boundaries — if a function is not in the list, it must be
357.   fully verified.
358. - When writing `assume_specification`, follow the audit checklist in
359.   Part 1 (Anti-Patterns, Verification Escape).

363. ## Part 3: View Abstraction Design
364. 
365. The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
366. specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
367. often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
368. for reference.
369. 
370. See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for the complete step-by-step guide
371. on View design, invariants, and method specifications.
372. 
373. 1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
374.    swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
375. 2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
376.    `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
377. 3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
378.    closed so implementation details don't leak.
379. 4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
380.    abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).
381. 5. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
382.    Put reusable spec helpers on the View type instead.
383. 
384. For full View design methodology, see the **view-design** skill.
385. 
386. ### Spec Transition Functions
387. 
388. For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
389. on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
390. (frame condition):
391. 
392. ```rust
393. impl FooView {
394.     pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
395.         FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
396.     }
397. }
398. // ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
399. ```
400. 
401. **Do NOT** also list individual field changes as separate ensures — the
402. spec transition already captures the complete state change.
403. 
404. When modifying a collection element without a spec transition, state the
405. frame explicitly:
406. `forall|i: int| i != changed_idx ==> new@[i] == old@[i]`
